THE ENGLISH COLONIES

FROM 1574 TO 1660.

THE

ENGLISH COLONIES

FROM 1574 TO 1660,

ACCORDING TO THE STATE PAPERS,

AND

EPISODE
OF BELGIAN EMIGRATION TO VIRGINIA,

BY

J. FELSENHART,
DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY AND LETTERS.

GHENT,
PRINTING AND LITHOGRAPHY OF L. HEBBELYNCK.
—
1867

FOREWORD.

The Anglo-Saxon race has constantly united two
elements seemingly irreconcilable at first glance: a love of
commercial transactions together with a keen interest in
intellectual and moral matters. True to this tradition,
the Queen's government, in agreement with
Parliament, had the fortunate and fruitful idea of
condensing within a vast framework, by means of
substantial analyses, all the documents of a nature
to shed vivid light on the history of Great
Britain; it is to this intelligent initiative that we
owe the publication of the State Papers. This vast
collection branches out across the entire historical
domain and will form, once it is complete,
an inexhaustible source of information and
details.

We must hasten to say, however, that given the state
in which the writer finds the materials in these State Papers,
he cannot aim at the grand proportions
of general history. By their very nature, the documents
scattered throughout the various national archives
serve only to illuminate and corroborate facts already known.
Valuable for lending support on certain points,
they would, most of the time, prove insufficient
if it were a matter of reconstructing, from one end to the other, the
immense framework of the historical edifice erected in

— VI —

the past through long series of writers. If we confine ourselves to ancient history alone, how many facts there are to correct! And yet, one may without presumption maintain that Herodotus, Tacitus, Thucydides, and Livy have given us a faithful and moving picture of Greek and Roman society. More precise documents, were it possible to obtain them, could at most serve only to refine certain details. The genius of these immortal masters has retraced everything, painted everything, generalized everything. Their manner is the very nerve of history. Could it be otherwise? General history and its various branches form the orbit within which humanity moves under the irresistible action of eternal and unchanging principles. It is the voice of God, great and powerful, echoing from age to age through the vast circle of the centuries. If we do not preserve the philosophical spirit within it, if the flashes of the philosophy of history do not illuminate it, it degenerates, descending from its radiant height to place itself humbly on the level of mere chronicles—a dull and insipid juxtaposition of facts. Today, in our age, when the most unbridled materialism has taken hold of hearts and minds, it is important to preserve for historical studies their civilizing mission of elevating man through the spectacle of man's greatness in the past.

But such care cannot be entrusted to crude historical empiricism. Instead of enlarging ideas, ennobling them, stirring them toward ideal aspirations, this colorless approach would end up crushing the intellect under an avalanche of juxtaposed facts, without coordination and, above all, without soul. For wherever the fact does not vibrate beneath the vivifying breath of writing—

— VII —

in vain, the fact becomes a brew that leads to
stupefaction. The style is the man, and history is
the writer of genius.

The Belgian legislator, through his law on higher
education, felt the necessity of preserving history's
dignity. This fortunate inspiration explains
the important place he assigned to the political history
of peoples, and the desire to instill in studious youth
firm principles that might guide them
rather than leading them astray in a maze of facts.

It is therefore evident that the State Papers, a mere aggregate
of cold analyses, are not sufficient resources
to allow one to contemplate such grandeur.
The idea we have just given explains the nature
of this work and the conditions under which
it was produced.

Within the lineage of historical branches, the history
of the colonies holds a place apart. It appeals
to the economist and the publicist. It is of
extreme importance.

At the dawn of history, civilization, departing from
the Orient, spread to Europe through sublime
adventurers who brought it from the farthest reaches
of Asia and Africa. In that age, the thickest
darkness prevented even the most profound and
most perceptive scholarship from bringing events
into full light. But in modern times, everything
changes. Then adventures follow a
certain method. They have a program. Sometimes
it consists of extending the market of the mother country,
opening new paths for speculators; sometimes,
though less often, of carrying to distant shores
religious doctrines or the spirit of sects.

— VIII —

From this point of view, the history of the English colonies
presents characteristics of the highest interest. It
teaches us that the greatness, the moral and political
amplitude of nations depends in large part on
the prosperity of their colonies, and that the glory of
the latter is intimately linked to the firm and
wise conduct of government.

Now the *State Papers* only reflect and echo
all this. They are sources of information
lacking the charm of detail; they are a dried-up
artery in the vast historical organism.

We find proof of this in the Belgian (Walloon)
and French emigration that went to reinforce,
at the beginning of the 17th century, the colonists of
Virginia. It is with a mysterious pleasure that one
looks back to that already distant era, when
compatriots abandoned the soil of Belgium
to go cultivate the vast wilderness of the United States.
The excited imagination is eager to know the
details of this Belgian *ver sacrum*, of this great event so
important for our history. Unfortunately the
*State Papers* provide us in this regard only
a few pale official documents. The circumstances
of this emigration perhaps live on in
legends, traditional memories, and a writer
fortunate enough to gather them could reconstruct
one of the most curious episodes of our
modern history. Who knows whether one day or another one of
our diplomatic agents might not have the good
fortune to make this precious discovery?

We hope for it, without daring to expect it.

I.

Summary: The meaning of trade and colonies from a philosophical point of view. — Assessment of English archives. — Queen Elizabeth, Hawkins, Drake, and Cavendish. — The committee for promoting voyages of adventure; Carlile. — Gilbert and the spirit of intolerance beyond the Atlantic. — Simon Ferdinando, Ralph Lane, Walsingham. — A scene of piracy.

The formation of human society has its root in an instinct. Everywhere, at the cradle of history, religious beliefs trace it back to a higher, metaphysical principle, and later philosophical systems take hold of it to explain it through the thousand paths of reason. Now, this instinct we call sociability. It is a propulsive force that drives man to unite with man, generations to graft themselves upon generations, and to fulfill, in ever-growing concentric circles, the supreme design of nature or of God—that is, the great epic of creation with its infinite varieties. Through this feeling, man is something, a shadow; without it, all moral or physical progress would lack any foundation. Thus, when one goes back through the ages, far back, beyond historical memory, one senses humanity cramped within the stage of its aspirations. It tries to spring forward
1

— 2 —

at the peak of its destinies, without the slightest awareness of
philosophical abstractions. Alas! already then, sociability,
that noble attribute of human collectivity, under the grip
of passions and the weight of vulgar interests, bent all too easily
in an environment that dulled its brilliance.
Having been intuitive, humanity becomes speculative,
in the economic sense of the word. It fixes upon
realities and uses commerce as a vehicle that
runs through its entire sphere of activity. At this period,
commerce—like its sister, industry, later on—has an
unconscious mission. It is the propagator and prime mover
of civilization through a radiation similar to the laws
of heat, and the heart of humanity would freeze if
commercial relations did not simultaneously enrich it
through the progressive accumulation of knowledge.

Perhaps a few examples drawn from general history
will support our ideas on the authority of the centuries.
When the Hellenic world, at the height of its glory, scattered
the known globe with its colonies, like so many
pearls reflecting the beautiful sky of the Orient, did not
Greece ennoble human instinct, or sociability? And the
Carthaginians? Despite the Semitic greed attributed to them,
by crossing the ocean in search of
treasures, they were still true pioneers in the service
of civilization, exactly like the Roman who, in the
shadow of his eagles, opening colonies in every corner
of the globe, seemed to wait on the edge of the precipice for the
barbarian German, who came in the 5th century, to relaunch in another
direction the decrepit chariot of Roman civilization. All
these facts stem from the sociability of man, and thus
the world comes into being. It develops, grows, bursts
and breaks apart only to reconstitute itself anew. Through these
various changes, historical epochs shine or fade.
They borrow from them a particular, individual

— 3 —

duel. Witness the modern times. Shining with a brilliance
borrowed from the past, they nourish themselves on a sap whose
luxuriant abundance has made the mustard seed into the gigantic
tree that shakes its rich harvest of fruits over all the earth.
Here the scene opens with nuances unknown to the ancient world.
In entering the fifteenth century, to continue its evolutions,
one would say that humanity is reborn at the spectacle of a new
creation. Enthusiasm animates it. From this moment on, man,
tormented by the spirit of adventure, sets out to discover the
unknown parts of his royal domain, while awaiting the moment
when he will embellish it with the enchantments of his genius.
Why do commerce and industry still await their epic? and who
will explain to us the reason why the noxious exhalations of the
battlefield excite the inspiration of the Homers and Virgils more
than the perfumed and picturesque theater of the colonies founded
by the commercial spirit of modern times?

But let us come down to real things. The mass of documents
condensed through analyses in the State Papers (1) is well suited
to tempt at least the imagination. With the Colonial Papers, one
of the subdivisions of this immense repository, one witnesses the
birth of all the English colonies. Just as the geologist, through
his labors, becomes an enthusiastic spectator of earthly revolutions,
so too, in searching through the British Archives, one feels
as though aboard one of those ships that carried in their holds
illustrious and intrepid adventurers, setting out to fasten to the
shores of America those first moorings whose transformation,
three centuries later, is called the transatlantic cable.

It goes without saying that we confine ourselves within the
restricted limits of the State Papers. It is with their aid that we

Annals of the Archaeological Academy of Belgium.

— 4 —

we shall attempt to sketch the history of the English colonies from
1574 to 1660.

Before the reign of Elizabeth, the English nation had not
yet acquired the supremacy at sea that we have since seen it hold.
In the Middle Ages, it was Italy's turn to exercise
maritime predominance. Later, when the Por-
tuguese and the Spanish, thanks to a combination of fortunate
circumstances, explored the seas and made their flags
prevail, the English, sharing in this the fate of other
nations, had to bow before the daring and fortune of
their rivals. Thus the English Archives, as regards the
colonial establishments, leave, before Elizabeth, much
to be desired. One finds there a veritable
scarcity of documents. The first one encounters in
the Colonial Papers dates from the year 1574. No doubt
Sir John Hawkins (1), Drake, and Cavendish, through their
adventures and discoveries, deserve pages often glorious
in the annals of the English navy, but our
scope compels us, at least, to defer the account of their
exploits (2).


(1) Hawkins, for example, made three voyages to the coasts of America; he
traded Black people for objects of little value, and of the six ships that
were destined for this inhuman traffic, the two largest belonged to
Queen Elizabeth, who did not throw profits to the dogs.

(2) In this work, we are not concerned with the archives analyzed
in the State Papers, bearing the title: Colonial series East Indies, China and
Japan. These curious documents derive from the Public Record Office, the British Mu-
seum, and the India Office. They form a special volume, spanning from 1513
to 1616, and relate to discoveries in the Northwest or other
passages to the Indies. One sees there the birth of the East India
Company and the beginnings of the factories. One then witnesses the gradual
development of English influence in the Orient, the birth of
England's commercial relations with Persia, China, and Japan, and
the breaking off of international relations with the last-named country, following
the death of an emperor and the inauguration of a new policy, in
which religious considerations weighed heavily in the balance.

The Calendar of State Papers, colonial series, 1574-1660, constitute a
large volume of 577 pages, which spans, as one can see, nearly a century. Res-

— 5 —

Thus, in 1574, a committee was created to encourage
voyages of adventure; it was composed of alderman Hart,
Spencer, W. Burrough, Hoddesdon, Towerson,
Slanghe, Stapers, Maye, John Castelin, and Leake.
This committee entered into communication with Mr. Carlile, whose
project consisted of exploring the northern parts
of America. According to this commission's opinion, it would be
good to send to those regions a hundred men who would
be obliged to stay there one year, to study the topography
of the country and its chief products. The expenses of
the undertaking would amount to four thousand pounds. The city of
Bristol offered a thousand of these, and the city of London would
undertake to cover the rest. Efforts would be made to secure
privileges for Mr. Carlile, and the conditions under
which other emigrants would be admitted to settle would be set. In
the patent that the queen would grant to the worthy adventurer, it
would be stipulated that it is entirely up to Mr. Carlile to
transport to America all those who expressed the
desire to go, provided they agreed to
remain there for a period of ten years. No one would be allowed to found
a settlement without having obtained a license for that purpose, nor
to live or trade within a radius of two hundred leagues
from the point where the governor had established his residence.
On March 22, 1574, a petition in line with this committee's
views was addressed to the queen; it bore the signa-
tures of sir Humfrey Gilbert, sir G. Peckham, Car-
lile, and sir Pic. Greenvile. It also requested
permission to go in search of unknown lands,
"fatally reserved," as the petitioners put it, "for England
and for the glory of Your Majesty."


[continuing from previous page] ...twenty-eight years until the revolution of 1688. It is likely that this
period will provide five more volumes, so abundant is the material. Indeed,
after the return of Charles II, the plantations became more populated and
more important; the documents relating to them naturally became more
frequent and more numerous.

— 6 —

Following this project, one finds a document indicating
that the adventurers were prompt in carrying it out. It
dates from 1580, and is of the greatest interest. It is a
fragmentary report from several persons who made
the transatlantic voyage. It speaks of the dispositions of
the Indian people, depicted as rather gentle, of the customs and
costumes of these natives. The authors of the account
did not fail to mention that the women of this region
are covered with gold leaves as with armor. They
also go into details of the strategy of these Indians.
As for their religion, they worship a demon, who commu-
nicates with them in the form of a calf. Then, they dwell
on the coronation ceremonies customary in
the region. A certain Champion, French by origin,
gave an Englishman a hundred silver coins in exchange for an
old Indian flag. The soil of this country is excellent,
they continue, especially along the banks of the Mai. They then
dwell on the ornithology, the fauna, and the hunting of beasts
as large as two of our oxen. In all the
huts one finds pearls. Around Sainte-Marie, there are
fire dragons that color the air red
when they fly. The streets are wider than those of
London. There are dining halls of crystal, with pillars
of solid silver, some even of gold. At the
source of the rivers, one sees nuggets of pure gold as large
as a fist. As for iron, there is abundance. Silkworms
are very numerous. A mountain, called
Banchoonan, which covers the northern part, at a
distance of about thirty leagues from the bay of Sainte-Marie,
is rich in mines.

The document whose analysis we present is nothing other
than a fairly detailed report. It is owed in part
to David Ingram and in part to Vererzamis, to Jacques Cartier,
to John Barros, to Thevett, and to John Waker. Sir Humphrey

— 7 —

Gilbert had been personally in communication with the last three.

In 1579, Simon Ferdinando, the man who was, so to speak, secretary Walsingham's agent (1), returned from that distant voyage "in the small frigate," without any other companion. Later, in 1580, John Waker and his associates discovered a silver mine near the Norumbega river.

In 1578, Queen Elizabeth had granted sir Humphrey Gilbert letters patent authorizing him to take possession of all lands not yet occupied by Christian princes and to establish settlements there. Gilbert rose to the level of his mission; but the measures he took to secure for the Church of England and the Queen the respect and affection of the colonists prove all too well that Protestantism, in the sixteenth century, wielded with barbaric skill the scourge of despotism and intolerance (2).

(1) This distinguished statesman, who plays so great a role in the State Papers, after undertaking rigorous studies and travels on the continent, managed to ingratiate himself into the good graces of William Cecil, and later succeeded in being appointed to the eminent post of Secretary of State and privy councillor to Queen Elizabeth. He refused to associate himself with Leicester's scheme, who reportedly would have liked to dispose of Mary, Queen of Scots, by poison—which would certainly prove something about him, since toward his rivals, the Catholics, he showed a furious intolerance. In the various courts of Europe, Leicester kept spies in his pay who enabled him to report to his virginal mistress everything that happened there. In politics one may listen at doors. How charming!

(2) Humphrey Gilbert is regarded by the English as the founder of their colonization of the West. He spread throughout his country a taste for discovery and sharpened the spirit of adventure. He was no less distinguished as an orator than as a soldier. He died in 1584 in a shipwreck, after having given admirable proof of courage and composure. One may reproach him for having let himself be too strongly drawn by veins of silver. After the silver, the deluge. Unfortunately, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and even later, the halo of science stimulated men far less than precious metals did. We, in the nineteenth century, have no right to complain. We surpass the discoverers of the sixteenth century in this respect, just as needle-guns surpass the modest wheel-lock musket! True progress is rare.

— 8 —

Ralph Lane, in his correspondence with Walsingham, goes into several details that are still quite interesting today. He writes to the latter, from Port Ferdinando, in Virginia, on August 12, 1580, that the return to England of Sir R. Grenville deprives him of the pleasure of going into particulars. He and his companions arrived late, it is true, in America; but their discoveries are so numerous, the products of the country so rare and so new, that the kingdom of Virginia, according to all the apothecaries (1), is without doubt the finest jewel in the English crown. So far not a single harmful plant has been discovered there. Its territory is vast, varied in terrain, and presents natural fortifications. As for the climate, it is extremely healthy; Port Ferdinando is accessible from only three sides: they have given these the names Trinity, Scarborough, and Ococan. The fleet ran aground there, and the Tiger very nearly was lost. Simon Ferdinando discovered the best harbor. It was named after him. It should be remembered that Ferdinando was captain and chief pilot of the fleet. With a simple fort, one could defend this port against the combined forces of Spain. The conquest of this country seems assured to Ralph Lane. Then, delivered from their enemies, from the tyranny of Spain and the papists, he and his companions will not allow anyone to hinder this most Christian enterprise, and closing in the biblical taste of the time: "God will ordain," he says, "that the ravens of the sky shall give food to His elect (2)."

On August 12, 1585, the same man also writes to Walsingham; but his letter offers no important particulars. The same is true of the one addressed, under the same

(2) Colonial Papers, page 3.

— 9 —

dated, to Sir Philip Sidney; he says in this last letter
that the strength of Spain comes to her from the treasures she
draws from her mines.

On September 8th of the same year, he writes again
to Secretary Walsingham. His whole letter deals with
Grenville's tyrannical methods. The colonists have dis-
covered a kind of wheat, producing grain and sugar at
the same time. They sent a sample of it to Sir
W. Raleigh. In the plains, the soil is fertile; the country
is inhabited by savages of a gentle character, who readily
yield to the beneficial influences of Christianity (1).

On October 29th, Grenville writes from Plymouth to Secretary
Walsingham. He informs him of his return to Europe.
He has fulfilled his mission, discovered a new country, to
which he gave the name of Virginia, and which he has amply
supplied with cattle, fruits, and plants. On his return, he
captured at sea a Spanish ship, coming from Santo Domingo,
loaded with ginger and sugar. He does not believe that the
Spaniards derive from this settlement pearls, silver,
and gold in such great quantity as is claimed.

A revolting act of piracy took place in 1596. We know
of it through a report by Sir Richard Clarke. It took place
on the coasts of Newfoundland, and three French ships
are said to have been guilty of the blackest
treachery. Michel de Sancé and Martin de Sancé invited
Rich. Clarke aboard, lavished courteous attentions on him,
and kept him for lunch. Clarke did not wish to be
outdone in politeness: in turn, he extended an invitation
to his hosts; but they declined the offer, on the pretext
that Michel de Sancé was confined to bed by a serious
illness. Clarke, unable to return the honor

(1) Colonial Papers, page 3.

— 10 —

which had been done to him, hastened at least to pay a visit to
Sancé. No sooner had he set foot in the sick man's cabin
than the French cried out: Rend vouz, rend vouz (1).
The Englishman yielded to force; he was taken prisoner along with his
companions. His captivity lasted nine days. After this time, his
ship was returned to him, but stripped of its cargo. In
the margin of this report are inscribed the eyewitnesses
of this scene: R. Clarke, Master Mat. Ryves and Phil. Fo-
byan, boatswains; Laun. Charke, surgeon, and seventy
others, "as well as many other names" (and many
others). This last detail removes from the document its character of
gravity. It recalls a bit too crudely ... et quibusdam
aliis [and certain others] (2). So much for the internal administration of the colonies under
Elizabeth.


II.

Summary: Origin of Virginia, Captain Newport, the young Pocahontas.
— John Smith in England, Lord de la Warr succumbs to fatigue. — The
lotteries, the press of young girls, and the sinister figure of Owen Evans. —
General Assembly of Virginia, laws and constitution, acts of cruelty.
— List of Walloons (Belgians) and French who emigrated to Virginia. —
Their nickname of vinerouns, their activity and their industry. — Massacre
of the colonists and plague. — Virginia, an integral part of the British
empire. — Efforts of the mother country to revive the colony. — Will. Berkeley
and the remarkable instructions of King Charles I. — Virginia under Crom-
well. — What it became under the restoration of Charles II.


The first and most important settlement that the
English made in America is without question that
of Virginia (3). The State Papers provide on this matter


(1) Spelling from the English report.
(2) Colonial Papers, page 4: and seventeen other names, "and many others."
(3) Present-day Virginia lies between 36°50' and 40°38' N. latitude
and 75°10' and 83°30' longitude. The first colonists settled there in 1607,
under the leadership of Captain John Smith, the same one mentioned further below.

— 11 —

numerous details, of a nature to illustrate in the most vivid
colors the origin of this fine colony. What strikes one in the
first place is the journal of Captain Newport, a curious piece
in several respects, which informs us, among other
particulars of piquant interest to his contemporaries,
that the president of the colony, Edward-Maria Wingfield,
in a battle fought against two hundred savages, escaped
as if by miracle, if it is true, as the facetious
captain attests, that a projectile passed through Wingfield's
beard without causing him the slightest scratch (had a
shot clean through his beard, yet escaped unhurt).

The description that Newport gives of this region and his
ethnographic observations are worthy of attention.
It is also in this document that one encounters for
the first time the name Pawatan, of the great Pawatan,
as he was called then, and who has been the subject of so many
romantic tales. In June 1616, Chamberlain writes to Carleton
that Sir Th. Dale has returned from Virginia with ten or twelve
natives of that country. Lord Carew, in his letter in the form
of a journal, adds that these natives were landed in
England, to be raised and initiated into European
civilization there. Among these savages, according to the same
account, is a person of accomplished beauty; it is Poca-
huntas, daughter of Pawatan, who was joined in marriage to an
Englishman named Rolfe. On January 18, 1617, Chamber-
lain writes from London to Carleton that the young Pocahuntas,
of Virginia, and one of her father's counselors were presented
to King James I and graciously received by the
monarch. At the masked ball they were given the best place.
These two personages were delighted with this novelty.
Pocahuntas, he says, will return to her homeland, assuredly
reluctantly. On March 29 of the same year, Chamber-
lain sends Carleton the portrait of the interesting savage,
informing him of the sad news that she had just died

— 12 —

at Gravesend (1), where she wished to embark to return
to Virginia.

A letter from the second president of the colony, Captain
John Radclyeffe, gives interesting news of the progress
made by this colonial settlement up to October 1609. It
reveals the sending to England of Captain John Smith (2),
the father of Virginia, to answer for the numerous misdeeds
he was guilty of.

A year later, Lord de la Warr and Sir George Somers,
writing from James Town (3) on June 15, give a striking
account of the storm that struck the fleet sent by the
English company to aid the faltering colony. After
lamentable incidents, the passengers finally arrive in that
town, "which is," they say, "a sad and deserted city
because of the great mortality that reigns there."

On his return to Europe (June 1611), Lord de la Warr
wrote a moving letter to Salisbury (4). He states in
melancholy terms that he is succumbing to the efforts he
has made to resist the illness that is wasting him away,
but that he has the firmest hope that the company will
succeed in founding the colony to which it has devoted
so much care and spent so much

butchered to be devoured. Pocahontas, despite the threats of a band of

(4) The most famous and most skillful minister of James I. He is known

of capital. Seven years later, this steadfast and fearless colonist died during the crossing from London to James-Town. The prosperity of the colony was not yet definitively assured.

To sustain this often-threatened enterprise, recourse was had to lotteries. This chancy way of raising funds sharpened the satirical wit of the Spaniards. To mock the English entrepreneurs, they said facetiously that the English were obliged to organize begging, but in vain, since the ruin of the plantation was an easy thing, according to the opinion of the ambassador of the Most Catholic King.

Despite these hostile sentiments, the growth of the colony continued steadily. It is true that no means that might ensure its success was neglected. The mayor and alderman of Canterbury received a pressing invitation from the Privy Council to recommend this worthy and Christian enterprise. Recourse was had to the impressment of young women, just as is done with sailors in time of maritime war. In a letter of 19 October 1618 to the Privy Council, Sir Edward Hent, justice of the peace of Somersetshire, complains of the shameful conduct of Owen Evans, a messenger of the Chamber, who had become, in that district, the terror of young women. To escape the practices of this official procurer of white flesh, forty of these poor creatures found themselves forced to leave their parishes and seek, in obscure hiding places, a refuge from the persecutions of this odious agent. That is not all. Children were torn from the parents of "the vile multitude" (superfluous) of the city, and were made to take the road to Virginia (1). The momentum was irre-

— 14 —

irresistible, ships followed one another without respite, loaded
with men and provisions.

Four years later, in 1616, Sir Th. Dale gave notice
to Lord Winwood of his departure, informing him at the same time
that he was leaving the colony pacified and prosperous.

In 1622, Wyatt (1), his successor, in a report to
the king, assured him that many cities of renown in the West
Indies were not comparable to the new State (many cities
of great rumour in the West Indies, established more than
sixty years, were not to be compared to Virginia).

On July 30, 1619, the first general assembly met in
Virginia. This was, as we see, a State born into
constitutional institutions. The governor was by right a
member of this embryonic parliament. He was assisted by a
councillor of State and two members or burgesses elected by
the corporations. The rest of the deputies were appointed by
the cities of James, Charles, Henry, Kiccowton, the
plantation of Captain John Martin, the township of Smythe,
the township of Martin, of Argoll, of Flowerdien, and the plantations
of Captains Lowne and Warde. The session was held
in the choir of the church. The first act of the assembly
was to decree a pound of tobacco as a tax to be levied

This request did not go unanswered. On August 11, 1621, the deputy John Ferrar wrote, on behalf of the Virginia Company, that there was no objection to admitting the request of the Walloons and the French, provided, however, that the number of these emigrants did not exceed three hundred, that they were willing to swear the oath of supremacy and conform to the rules of the established Church. Under these conditions, they would be granted plots of land in sufficient number across the various cities, towns, and corporations of Virginia. These new colonists, who were given the nickname of "vignerons" (vinerouns for vinedressers), rendered the most outstanding services to their new homeland. Originally, most of the planters only engaged in tobacco cultivation; the king recommended that they raise silkworms and manufacture fabrics from this precious material, adding that "it is a rich and solid product, preferable to tobacco (1)." Only the vignerons responded to His Majesty's call. Settled at Elizabeth City, they devoted themselves actively to raising silkworms, and later it was said that the unfortunate Charles I, at his coronation, wore a garment whose silk had come from this distant region.

The colonists of Virginia lived for a long period on the best terms with the natives of this country. They lived in extreme security, enjoying happy days, full of confidence, in scattered houses situated at long distances from one another. Summary: Once again the Bermudas or the Somers Islands. — Shipwreck and famine. — Lord De la Warr and Somers. — Complaints of the House of Commons. — Jamaica. — Penn and Venables. — A plan for colonial reorganization submitted to the king by James, Earl of Marlborough. — Tender and meticulous care.

The Bermudas or the Somers Islands have already passed before our eyes in this vast colonial panorama. The State Papers devote interesting pages to them. One of the most remarkable documents is the letter from Somers himself, "that good old gentleman," as Lord De la Warr is pleased to call him. It is addressed from James-Town, in Virginia, on June 15, 1609, to Salisbury, and dispels all uncertainty regarding the Somers Islands, of which we have, moreover, already spoken above. During the crossing to Virginia, says Somers (1), a violent storm broke out a hundred leagues from the Bermudas, and scattered the whole fleet. The ship carrying him sprang a leak. From then on the adventurers faced the greatest dangers. From July 23 to 28, 1610, a hundred men were employed at the pumps, day and night. On July 28, which was a Friday, they sighted the island of Bermuda. Somers's ship ran aground a quarter of a mile from the coast. No one perished. Part of the goods was even saved, but the supply of bread was lost. Between July 28 and May 10, 1610 [sic], the shipwrecked survivors, redoubling their activity and energy, built two small boats, which allowed them to leave the Bermudas on May 13 and set sail for Virginia, where they landed on the 23rd of that month, numbering one hundred and forty persons, men and women. At Cape Henry they were told of a terrible famine afflicting James-Town. They...

CONCLUSION.

These are the most salient facts that the State-Papers reveal to us regarding the causes that brought about the numerous discoveries of this period and the immediate effects produced by the dissemination across the globe of countless colonial establishments. Colonies are born, as we have said, of an innate sense of expansion, ingrained in man, of an instinct in a word; they are the manifestation, through physical and perceptible effects, of a need that relentlessly torments his being and stirs him in his very essence. When a nation, driven by its instincts, dreams of establishing its supremacy at sea, or rather of planting the markers that lead to it, one can be certain that it is under the breath of an energetic principle, steeped in destiny, which pushes it toward lofty fates. England, so admirably situated to become a maritime power, only became conscious of its mission at the very beginning of modern times. Before this period, it was in this respect in a relative state of inferiority. But after the great moral and religious upheaval that marks the 16th century, the genius of the English nation reflected itself in the mirror of its internal politics, and, aided by its national temperament, it raised England to that height from which it contemplated, for a century and a half, the convulsions that shook it while purifying it and which forced it to found its institutions upon the rock of liberty, unmoved amid the storms. This was a memorable stage in the annals of humanity. Thanks to the infinite scattering of its colonies

across every point of the globe, constitutional institutions had their transatlantic shipping line. From then on, liberty was able to move about. Under the action of irresistible currents that unleash passions into tumult and that cause human aspirations to pass from the extreme of moral greatness to the extreme of abjection, liberty went to plant its standards in the New World, where we first see it chained to the trading posts of the mother country, and then breaking its chains to shine forth with that majestic splendor which man, once escaped from the hands of the Creator, must surely have possessed. Admirable chain of events! The greedy merchant risks his days for often fleeting profit, governments cast beyond the seas populations whose religious sentiments they fear; genius, astonished at feeling cramped in its own homeland, braves the Ocean in search of wider horizons, and from all these principles of dispersion, from these disparate elements, there results a harmonious whole that preserves the races with their particular stamps, and endows the world with new societies. Great Britain—whose impending fall some gloomy minds celebrate in advance—Great Britain, identified with these general laws of history, has realized, developed, and, as it were, given material form to its distinctive genius, the type of its nationality, through the creation of its colonies. If it is true, as is claimed, that this country has today reached the height of its ambition, that it has attained the maximum of its greatness, it will have bequeathed to statesmen a fine example to follow and a lesson: it tells them, with the great voice of history, that the secret of the strength of nations lies in Neptune's trident placed at the service of free institutions.

Germany, dislocated for three centuries under the rod of the France of Richelieu, ever watchful to sow division there so that the Eagle of Germania might continually be forced to take its flight toward the mountains, that learned

— 91 —

country, this scientific hub, perhaps the most complete and
most active that the universe has produced, has barely freed itself
from the constraints in which the treaties held it, than it dreams of the
great road of humanity, that it dreams of creating a
navy to organize the immensity of its varied forces.
Starting from principles opposed to those which have shaped the life of
free England, Germany will logically arrive in
the future, if it persists in this path, at opposite results. The
absolute military regime is a primitive regime that imposes
itself upon nations in their infancy; it is found at
the origin of societies, when man worships brute force
and when right appears to him under the sinister and
mysterious aspect of the divinities of India and Persia. It follows
from this that such a regime, applied constantly to a nation,
however vigorous it may otherwise be, causes it to degenerate
into a political machine that crushes, demolishes, and kills, unless
events, political upheavals, come to neutralize the disastrous effect
of this governmental nature. What would be the consequences of the
maritime superiority of a people shaped by such a regime?
If it ever succeeded in founding or conquering colonies,
the subjection of man to the rigid laws of the camps
would, without doubt, under its domination, be the sublime
of the conceptions of the mind. For such is the power of this
expansive force of colonies, that they reflect everywhere
the political, moral, and religious tendencies of the
mother country. If, at the very moment when its genius creates around
it numerous colonies, as we have seen arise
in the preceding pages, the mother country has opened
its heart to these pure tendencies of humanity, then it
deposits here and there across the globe seeds of liberty that
will be the future of generations. In the opposite case, we
have everything to fear; with time and the passions of men
aiding, barbarism would once more bury the human race

— 92 —

beneath the foul mud produced by Asiatic institutions based on violence, arbitrariness, and contempt for human dignity.

The founding of colonies is therefore an entire moral and philosophical lesson. It is the living picture of this insatiable need, of this fortunate necessity for man to develop himself. Peoples who rightly take pride in their free and rational institutions are strengthened by the sight of accomplished deeds, by the idea that humanity has its reason and its root in the mission imposed upon it to fulfill a duty, and that this duty is connected to the primordial plan of creation, of which it is but a ray of light.
